course.title: AP Precalculus
course.description: Build the function toolkit that calculus depends on: how quantities change together, polynomial and rational functions, exponential and logarithmic models, and trigonometric and polar functions.
course.previewDescription: Study how outputs change with inputs, then use polynomial, rational, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions to describe patterns and build models.

unit.title: Polynomial and Rational Functions
unit.description: See how outputs change with inputs, then use rates of change, zeros, end behavior, asymptotes, and holes to describe polynomial and rational functions and build models from them.

quiz.title: Unit 1 FRQ 4: Modeling a non-periodic context (Topics 1.7 to 1.14)
quiz.headline: Build a rational model from two conditions, interpret an average rate of change, and explain a limitation.
quiz.promptTitle: Free response 4 · Modeling a non-periodic context · graphing calculator
quiz.prompt: A company makes custom water bottles. The average cost per bottle, in dollars, for an order of n bottles is modeled by A(n) = (a + bn)/n, where a is a fixed setup cost in dollars and b is the cost in dollars of making each bottle. For an order of 20 bottles the average cost is $13 per bottle, and for an order of 80 bottles the average cost is $7 per bottle.
quiz.instructions: Part A style: a graphing calculator is required. Show the work that leads to each answer; answers without supporting work may not earn credit where work is requested. Avoid rounding intermediate values, and give decimal approximations accurate to three places after the decimal point unless the part says otherwise. Unless otherwise specified, the domain of a function f is the set of all real numbers x for which f(x) is a real number.
quiz.note: Original practice question written in the AP Precalculus free-response format (6 points, parts A to C). Scoring is self-assessed with the point-by-point rubric. It is not an official AP question or an official AP score.

scaffold.label: Show work
scaffold.text: Write the setup, such as the expression you evaluate or the equation you solve, before the answer.

scaffold.label: Use notation
scaffold.text: Use limit notation, interval notation, and units exactly where a part asks for them.

scaffold.label: Justify
scaffold.text: When a part says give a reason or explain, refer to the given values or the context.

responseFields.label: Part A (i)
responseFields.prompt: A (i). Use the given data to write two equations that can be used to find the values of the constants a and b in the expression for A(n).
responseFields.placeholder: Show the work that leads to your answer, then state the answer with any units or notation the part asks for.

responseFields.label: Part A (ii)
responseFields.prompt: A (ii). Find the values of a and b.
responseFields.placeholder: Show the work that leads to your answer, then state the answer with any units or notation the part asks for.

responseFields.label: Part B (i)
responseFields.prompt: B (i). Use the given data to find the average rate of change of A from n = 20 to n = 80 bottles. Show the computations that lead to your answer, and include units.
responseFields.placeholder: Show the work that leads to your answer, then state the answer with any units or notation the part asks for.

responseFields.label: Part B (ii)
responseFields.prompt: B (ii). Interpret the meaning of your answer from part B (i) in the context of the problem.
responseFields.placeholder: Show the work that leads to your answer, then state the answer with any units or notation the part asks for.

responseFields.label: Part C (i)
responseFields.prompt: C (i). Write and solve an equation whose solution gives the number of bottles n for which the average cost is $6 per bottle.
responseFields.placeholder: Show the work that leads to your answer, then state the answer with any units or notation the part asks for.

responseFields.label: Part C (ii)
responseFields.prompt: C (ii). A manager claims that a large enough order will bring the average cost to $5 per bottle. Use the model to explain whether the claim is correct. Refer to the end behavior of A in your explanation.
responseFields.placeholder: Show the work that leads to your answer, then state the answer with any units or notation the part asks for.

rubric.label: A (i) Two equations
rubric.guidance: Earn the point for (a + 20b)/20 = 13 and (a + 80b)/80 = 7, or the equivalent a + 20b = 260 and a + 80b = 560.

rubric.label: A (ii) Values of a and b
rubric.guidance: Earn the point for a = 160 and b = 5, so A(n) = (160 + 5n)/n.

rubric.label: B (i) Average rate of change
rubric.guidance: Earn the point for (A(80) − A(20))/(80 − 20) = (7 − 13)/60 = −0.1 dollar per bottle, per bottle.

rubric.label: B (ii) Interpretation
rubric.guidance: Earn the point for: from n = 20 to n = 80 bottles, on average, the average cost per bottle decreased at a rate of $0.10 per additional bottle ordered.

rubric.label: C (i) Equation and value of n
rubric.guidance: Earn the point for (160 + 5n)/n = 6, giving 160 + 5n = 6n and n = 160 bottles.

rubric.label: C (ii) Explanation
rubric.guidance: Earn the point for explaining that A(n) = 5 + 160/n > 5 for every n > 0, and lim n→∞ A(n) = 5, so the average cost gets arbitrarily close to $5 but never reaches it; the claim is incorrect.

quiz.modelResponse:
A (i). Because A(20) = 13 and A(80) = 7, two equations are (a + 20b)/20 = 13 and (a + 80b)/80 = 7, that is, a + 20b = 260 and a + 80b = 560.

A (ii). Subtracting gives 60b = 300, so b = 5. Then a = 260 − 100 = 160. A(n) = (160 + 5n)/n.

B (i). (A(80) − A(20))/(80 − 20) = (7 − 13)/60 = −0.1. The average rate of change is −0.1 dollar per bottle, per additional bottle.

B (ii). From an order of 20 bottles to an order of 80 bottles, on average, the average cost per bottle decreased at a rate of $0.10 for each additional bottle ordered.

C (i). A(n) = 6, so (160 + 5n)/n = 6. Then 160 + 5n = 6n, and n = 160 bottles.

C (ii). A(n) = 5 + 160/n. For every n > 0, 160/n > 0, so A(n) > 5. As n increases without bound, 160/n approaches 0, so lim n→∞ A(n) = 5. The average cost gets arbitrarily close to $5 per bottle but never equals $5, so the manager's claim is incorrect.
quiz.alternateModel: In A (ii) a graphing calculator may be used to solve the system. In C (ii) it is also correct to solve (160 + 5n)/n = 5, which gives 160 = 0, a contradiction, and to connect that to the horizontal asymptote y = 5.
commonErrors: Writing a + 20b = 13 instead of multiplying the average cost by the number of bottles.
Reporting the change in average cost, −6, instead of dividing by 60 bottles.
Interpreting −0.1 as the cost of one bottle.
Claiming the average cost reaches $5 for a very large order.
Leaving out units or 'on average' in the interpretation.
